blocks.title: How many species are there on Earth and How many in India?
blocks.text:
Estimates of species diversity do not give any figures for prokaryotes because: (i) Conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species. (ii) Many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.

India:

  • World area – 2.4%
  • Biodiversity – 8.1% (Among 12 mega diversity countries of the world)

blocks.title: Question.1
blocks.question:
According to Robert May, the global species diversity is about:
(1) 7 million
(2) 1.5 million
(3) 20 million
(4) 50 million
blocks.answer:
Ans: (1)

Explanation:

According to Robert May, a renowned ecologist, the global species diversity is estimated to be around 7 million species. However, it is believed that the total number of species on Earth could be much higher, with many species still undiscovered, particularly in remote areas and among microorganisms. The estimates often range widely due to the complexity of biodiversity and the challenges in species identification.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
What is so special about tropics that might account for their greater species diversity?

1. Tropical latitudes had a long evolutionary time for species diversification.

2. Constant environment promotes niche specialisation and leads to a greater species diversity

3. More solar energy available in the tropics, higher productivity; contribute indirectly to greater diversity.

(ii) Species - Area relationship:

Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.

Value of Z :

(a) Z = 0.1 to 0.2 (Regardless of the taxonomic group of the region)

(b) Z = 0.6 to 1.2 (Very large areas like the entire continents)

(c) Z = 1.15 [For frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in the tropical forests

(iii) The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem :

$\text{Species diversity} \uparrow \rightarrow \text{Stability} \uparrow \ (\text{Showed in experiments by David Tilman})$

Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich) :    • Airplane (Ecosystem)
    • Rivets (Species)
    • Rivets on the wings (Key species)
Stable community:      • Productivity constant
      • Resistant
      • Resilient

modules.name: Loss of Biodiversity/ Causes of Biodiversity Loss

blocks.title: Core Concept: Loss of Biodiversity
blocks.text:
Accusing fingers point to human activities :-

• Tropical Pacific Islands extinction of more than 2000 native birds

• IUCN Red List (2004) extinction-784 species in last 500 years

• Last twenty years-disappearance of 27 species

Examples of recent extinctions :-

  • Dodo →Mauritius
  • Quagga →Africa
  • Thylacine → Australia
  • Steller's Sea Cow → Russia
• Three subspecies of tiger → Bali, Javan, Caspian

Threat of extinction :-

  • Amphibian species → 32 percent
  • Gymnosperm species→ 31 percent
  • Mammal species → 23 percent
  • Bird species → 12 percent
  • During the long period (> 3 billion years) since the origin on earth - five episodes of mass extinction of species.
  • Presently the sixth episode is in progress and difference is in the rate as it is 100 to 1,000 times faster

blocks.title: Causes of Biodiversity Losses(The Evil Quartet)
blocks.text:
Habitat loss and fragmentation :-

  • Most important cause
  • Tropical rain forests once covering 14 percent, now no more than 6 percent
  • When large habitats are broken up into small fragments due to human activities, mammals and birds are badly affected, leading to population declines.
Over-exploitation :-

  • 'Need' turns to 'greed'
  • Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon
Alien species invasions :-

  • The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria leads to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake.
  • Invasive weed species in India like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia).
  • The recent illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus threat to the indigenous catfishes.
Co-extinctions :-

  • Mutualism (obligatory way)
  • Host specific parasites

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Biodiversity Conservation
blocks.text:
Why Should We Conserve Biodiversity?

Narrowly utilitarian argument

  • Direct economic benefits from nature
  • Food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and products of medicinal importance.
  • More than 25 percent of the drugs sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants.
  • 'Bioprospecting' - exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance.
Broadly utilitarian argument

  • The dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 percent of the total oxygen in the earth’s atmosphere.
  • Pollination
  • The aesthetic pleasures of walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in full bloom or waking up to a bulbul’s song in the morning.
The ethical argument

  • Philosophically or spiritually, we need to realise that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it may not be of current or any economic value to us. We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.
How do we conserve biodiversity?

TWO approaches: (i) In Situ Conservation

(ii) Ex-situ Conservation

(i) In Situ Conservation

Insitu (on site conservation) [When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected – like we save the entire forest to save the tiger

A. Biodiversity Hotspots

  • Very high levels of species richness, high degree of endemism, accelerated habitat loss
  • Biodiversity hotspots in the world are 34
  • Three of these hotspots - Western Ghat and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya cover our country's exceptionally high biodiversity regions.
  • Although all the biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area, the number of species they collectively harbour is extremely high and strict protection of these hotspots could reduce the on going mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.
B. Biosphere reserves - 14
C. National parks - 90
D. Wildlife sanctuaries -448
E. Sacred groves
    • India also has a history of religions and cultural traditions that emphasise the protection of nature. Such sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghats regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.
    • In Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.

(ii) Ex-situ Conservation

Ex-situ (off site conservation) [In this approach, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special settings where they can be protected and given special care]

A. Zoological parks

B. Botanical gardens

C. Wildlife safari parks

D. Cryopreservation techniques

E. Seed banks.

Special Points:

  • The Earth Summit' held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits.
  • In a follow-up, the World Summit on Sustainable development held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa
